summary: Describes a clock service offered by DCNET hosts, meant for clock synchronization and measuring one-way delay with cooperating hosts. It used timestamp messages from the proposed ICMP, and briefly also GGP echo messages for compatibility. This RFC is historic.

plainLanguage.summary: DCNET hosts offered a service for comparing clocks and measuring network delay. This RFC explains the timestamp messages and how a host can use their reply.

questions: how did the dcnet internet clock service work
how did ics measure network delay
what time units did rfc 778 use
subtitle: A DCNET service for clock synchronization and network-delay measurements.

tldr.problem: Cooperating hosts needed time references and a way to measure delay across the Internet.
tldr.mechanism: The service uses ICMP Timestamp or, temporarily for compatibility, GGP Echo datagrams. The sender supplies timestamps and the receiving host records receipt and reply times.
tldr.outcome: RFC 778 is Historic. It describes the DCNET service and methods for estimating one-way and round-trip delay.

today: RFC 778 is marked Historic in the unit metadata. The RFC describes an early DCNET clock and delay-measurement service.

sections.title: The DCNET Clock Service
sections.content:
The Internet Clock Service (ICS) was provided by DCNET hosts for clock synchronization and one-way delay measurements with cooperating Internet hosts. It used Timestamp and Timestamp Reply messages from the proposed ICMP, and also GGP Echo messages for a limited compatibility period.

These datagrams were treated differently from ordinary user datagrams and bypassed certain internal queues in gateways and hosts. The RFC presents the service as a way to encourage similar support elsewhere so its usefulness could be assessed.
sections.plainLanguage: DCNET offered special messages for hosts to compare time and estimate how long data takes to travel. These messages bypassed some normal queues.

sections.title: Timestamps and Replies
sections.content:
An ICS datagram contains an Internet header and an ICS header with type, code, sequence, and three timestamps. The sender fills all three timestamp fields before sending. The receiver records the arrival time and the time it forwards the reply, changes the type to the relevant reply type, and leaves the other fields unchanged.

Timestamps are milliseconds from midnight UT in 32-bit fields, with calculations ordinarily made modulo a day. The RFC gives a total datagram length of 36 octets, including the 20-octet Internet header and excluding the local-network leader.
sections.plainLanguage: The message records when it started, when the other host received it, and when that host sent it back. The sender can compare these times with the reply's arrival.

sections.title: Measuring Delay and Correcting Clocks
sections.content:
The sender labels the reply timestamps t1, t2, and t3, and records its arrival time as t4. The delay to the DCNET host is t2 minus t1; the return delay is t4 minus t3. Their sum gives the round-trip delay excluding internal processing at the DCNET host, and clock offsets cancel in that round-trip calculation.

The RFC identifies COMSAT-WWV as the designated time reference, using a Spectracom radio clock receiving WWVB time. It describes commands on COMSAT-GAT for retrieving current host offsets and the radio-clock status.
sections.plainLanguage: By comparing send, receive, and return times, a host can estimate each leg of a trip. The designated DCNET clock also supplies offsets for correcting other hosts' readings.
